title: The dangers of using proprietary LLMs for research

paragraphs.text: The release of ChatGPT at the end of 2022 thrust large language models (LLMs) into the limelight. By enabling its users to query the model directly in natural language, ChatGPT democratized access to these models — a welcome development. Since then, ChatGPT and similar tools such as Bard, Claude and Bing AI have shown their versatility and efficiency on a wide variety of tasks.

Social scientists have been quick to embrace these models. They have used these LLM-based AI assistants to summarize research articles, to debug code, and even to emulate survey participants, experimental subjects or agents in computer simulations1. Researchers have also adopted them to annotate texts. By passing a simple prompt to the machine, they can now sort through thousands of documents. They can do so rapidly, precisely, and according to their own coding scheme2. The promise is, indeed, alluring.
